title: Scales of production
needs: Say how the type of product, quality and quantity decide the method of production.
Describe batch, one-off, mass and continuous production, with examples.
Give the benefits and drawbacks of each scale of production.
Explain what a prototype is and why one is made.

doNow.q: Give two products that are made by batch production.
doNow.a: Any two of: clothing, baked goods, newspapers, electrical goods.

doNow.q: How long does continuous production run for?
doNow.a: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

doNow.q: Why would a factory use CNC wood turning to make 30 chair legs?
doNow.a: Every leg is accurately sized and identical, so they fit and match.
Job losses, high set-up cost, no human decision making, or workers need new skills to maintain it.

clues: I run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
I'm highly automated, so I only need a small workforce.
Oil refineries and blast furnaces use me.

items.text: Making a set quantity of consistent products to a quality standard.
Clothing, baked goods, newspapers and electrical goods.

chunks.label: Mass production
chunks.summary: Standardised products made in large quantities on automated lines.

written.q: Describe the main features of batch production.
points: A set quantity of consistent products is made to a quality standard.
Products are made in large batches, which reduces the cost per item.
Templates or moulds are used to keep products consistent.
Each batch is tested for quality and uniformity.
Machinery may need recalibrating or stopping between batches, causing downtime.
written.model: Batch production makes a set quantity of consistent products to a quality standard. Making them in large batches reduces the cost of each item, and templates or moulds keep every product the same. Each batch is tested for quality and uniformity, but machinery may need recalibrating or stopping between batches, which causes downtime.

written.q: Explain why a designer makes a prototype before a product goes into production.
points: To evaluate and test the design.
To confirm how the product will be made (the methods).
To confirm what the product will cost to make.
written.model: A prototype lets the designer evaluate and test the design before it is made in any quantity. It also confirms the methods that will be used to make it and what it will cost.

written.q: Explain why mass production lowers the cost of making each mobile phone.
points: Phones are standardised and made in large quantities.
Automated processes and assembly lines make high volumes efficiently.
Automated assembly lines need fewer workers.
Set-up costs for machinery or robots are high, but they are spread over a large number of phones.
So the cost per unit is reduced.
written.model: Mobile phones are standardised, so they can be made in very large quantities on automated assembly lines, which make high volumes efficiently and need fewer workers. The automated machinery and robots are expensive to set up, but those costs are spread over a large number of phones, so the cost of making each one is reduced.
written.note: 1 mark per linked point, up to 4.

written.q: Compare one-off production with mass production.
points: One-off makes a single item; mass production makes large quantities.
One-off items are often bespoke, made to a client's brief; mass-produced items are standardised.
One-off relies on a high level of skilled craftsmanship; mass production is automated and needs fewer workers.
One-off has a high cost of production; mass production spreads costs over many products, so the cost per unit is low.
One-off has high build quality; mass production makes high volumes efficiently.
written.model: One-off production makes a single item, often bespoke to a client's brief, while mass production makes large quantities of standardised products. One-off items rely on a high level of skilled craftsmanship, but mass production uses automated assembly lines and needs fewer workers. One-off items are costly to make, whereas mass production spreads its costs over many products, so each one costs less.
written.note: 1 mark per valid comparison point, up to 4.

written.q: A furniture company makes one-off, bespoke oak tables. It plans to batch produce a range of standard tables instead. Evaluate this decision.
points: Making tables in large batches would reduce the cost of each table.
Templates or moulds would keep every table in the batch consistent.
Each batch would be tested for quality and uniformity.
But machinery may need recalibrating or stopping between batches, causing downtime.
Tables would no longer be bespoke, made to each client's brief.
One-off tables have high build quality and skilled craftsmanship, but are costly to make.
Justified conclusion, e.g. batch production suits a lower-cost standard range; one-off suits clients who want a bespoke table and will pay more.
written.model: Batch producing the tables would reduce the cost of each one, and using templates would keep every table in a batch consistent, with each batch tested for quality and uniformity. However, machinery may need recalibrating or stopping between batches, causing downtime. The company would also lose the bespoke service: one-off tables are made to each client's brief with a high level of skilled craftsmanship and build quality, although they cost more to make. Batch production is the better choice if the company wants to sell a standard range at a lower cost, but it should keep one-off production for clients who want a bespoke table and will pay more for it.

levels.text: Detailed, balanced points on both sides, with a justified conclusion.
Some points, mostly on one side, or a conclusion that isn't justified.

written.note: Tick the points made, then use the levels under the model answer to decide the mark.

written.q: Describe the main features of continuous production.
points: The process runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Machinery is set up to make large volumes of a single item.
Processes are highly automated, with a small workforce.
It is very expensive to set up, run and stop.
Used for products such as steel, cement, petrochemicals and household chemicals.
written.model: Continuous production runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with machinery set up to make large volumes of a single item, such as steel or cement. The processes are highly automated, so only a small workforce is needed, but the industries that use it are very expensive to run.
